STAT210 · NMBU · learn it from zero

Forty Fish

The whole course, taught through one real experiment, with the actual graphs. Nothing is assumed. Every symbol is introduced before it is used, and every number is turned back into a fact about the fish.

Read this one straight through · about 45 minutes

Before we startWhat this is, and why

My other documents for you are reference documents. They are good for looking something up once you already understand it. They are close to useless for learning it in the first place.

This one is different. It follows one experiment from the raw measurements to the final conclusion, and every idea in the course appears only at the moment that story needs it. You end up understanding one experiment completely — and it turns out that is the same thing as understanding the course.

Then, at the end, there is a picture gallery: every kind of graph you will meet, shown twice — once when things are fine and once when they are broken — so you know what you are looking at.

How to read this

Do not skip the pictures. Every graph here is made from the real data, not drawn to look nice. Under each one is an orange box telling you exactly what to look at. That box is the point of the picture.

If a sentence loses you, it is my fault, not yours. Keep going — most things are explained twice, once in words and once in a picture.

Step 1Forty fish and a question

A fish farm has a problem. Some of their trout are anaemic — their blood does not carry enough oxygen. A researcher wants to know whether adding a drug called sulfamerazine to the feed helps.

So he does this:

  • He takes 40 trout.
  • He splits them into 4 groups of 10, completely at random.
  • Group 1 gets no drug. Groups 2, 3 and 4 get 5 g, 10 g and 15 g of it.
  • After 35 days he measures haemoglobin in each fish's blood — the stuff that carries oxygen. More is better.

That is the entire experiment. Now here is every measurement he got.

Look at this before reading on. Cover the rest of the page. Do the four groups look different to you? Where would you put your money? Most people looking at this say the first group looks lower than the other three — and that turns out to be exactly the right answer. Your eye is already doing statistics. The rest of this document is about making that judgement precise, and knowing when to trust it.
The thing the whole course is about

Look at the very first group — the fish that got no drug at all. Their haemoglobin ranges from about 5.5 to 8.6. That is a big spread, and every one of those fish had exactly the same treatment.

So fish differ from each other for reasons that have nothing to do with the drug. Genetics, size, luck.

That means when you compare two groups and see a difference, there are always two possible explanations: the drug did something, or you just happened to scoop up better fish. The entire subject exists to tell those two apart.

Step 2Look at it properly first

Before any calculation, statisticians draw a boxplot. It is a way of summarising each group so you can compare them at a glance.

Boxplot "box plot"

A summary of one group of numbers, drawn as a box. The thick line in the middle is the median — half the fish are above it, half below. The box holds the middle half of the fish. The whiskers reach out to the rest. Occasional dots beyond the whiskers are unusual individuals.

You use it to compare groups: are the boxes at different heights, and are they equally tall?

Two things to notice. First, the 0 g box sits lower than the other three — that is the possible drug effect. Second, and just as important, all four boxes are about the same height. That means the groups are similarly spread out, which is something you are required to check later. You have just done that check by eye.

Step 3The one idea in the whole course

Here is the idea everything else is built on. Take any single fish. Ask: why does it have the haemoglobin it has?

The answer is broken into three pieces:

  1. Start at the overall average of all 40 fish. That is 8.56. It is roughly what any trout has.
  2. Adjust for its group. The 5 g group averages 9.33, which is 0.77 above the overall average. So being in the 5 g group is worth +0.77.
  3. Adjust for the individual fish. This particular fish measured 11.9, but its group averages 9.33. So it is +2.57 above its own group, for reasons nothing to do with the drug.

Add them up: 8.56 + 0.77 + 2.57 = 11.90. Exactly what was measured.

Now here is that same idea drawn on all 40 fish at once.

This is the most important picture in the document. Look at the lengths. The green arrows — the drug effect — are short. The red lines — individual fish variation — are long. The noise is bigger than the signal. And yet, as you will see, the drug effect is still real. Learning how that can be true is what the next few steps are for.
μ, τ and ε "mew", "tow", "ep-si-lon"

These three Greek letters are the three pieces you just saw. Statisticians write the whole idea as one line:

y = μ + τ + ε a measurement = the overall average + the effect of its group + its own randomness

That is it. That line is called the model, and when a lecturer says "the model" this is what they mean. It is not a prediction machine — it is a claim about where each number came from.

Step 4Turning arrows into one number

We have 40 green arrows and 40 red lines. To compare "signal" against "noise" we need one number for each.

The obvious idea is to add up all the arrow lengths. That fails immediately, and it is worth seeing why.

Why you cannot just add them up

Some arrows point up, some point down. In the 0 g group the effect is negative (−1.36); in the 5 g group it is positive (+0.77). Add them and they cancel.

In fact they cancel exactly — the group effects always add to zero, by construction. So "total effect" is always 0, which tells you nothing.

The fix is to square everything first. Squaring makes negatives positive: (−2)² = 4, and (+2)² = 4 as well. So squaring measures how far without caring which way. Then you can add.

That is the only reason the course is full of squares. It is not deep. It is a trick to stop plus and minus cancelling out.

So: square every green arrow, add them up. Square every red line, add them up.

SIGNAL = 26.80     NOISE = 56.47     TOTAL = 83.27 26.80 + 56.47 = 83.27 — the two pieces add up exactly to the whole. Nothing is lost, nothing counted twice.
Sum of squares — SS "S S", or "sum of squares"

A total of squared distances. Just a number that means "how much variation is sitting here".

SSTr — "S S treatment" — the signal total, 26.80.
SSE — "S S error" — the noise total, 56.47.
SST — "S S total" — everything, 83.27.

"Error" does not mean anybody made a mistake. It means variation the drug cannot explain. It is an unfortunate word and it is standard.

Straight away this tells you something. Of all the variation in these 40 fish, 26.80 out of 83.27 — about 32% — is explained by which dose they got. The other 68% is fish being fish.

Step 5Making the two numbers comparable

Tempting next move: 26.80 versus 56.47, so noise wins, so nothing is happening. That reasoning is wrong, and understanding why is the hardest idea so far.

Why 26.80 and 56.47 cannot be compared directly

The noise total was built by adding up contributions from 40 fish. The signal total was built from only 4 group averages.

The noise number has far more things feeding into it, so it will be bigger almost regardless of whether there is any real noise. It wins on sheer volume.

Think of two shopping bags. One has 40 items, one has 4. The 40-item bag weighs more. That tells you nothing about whether its contents are heavy — for that you need weight per item.

So we need signal per unit of information, and noise per unit of information.

The "units of information" have a name that sounds much scarier than the idea.

Degrees of freedom — df "D F", or "degrees of freedom"

How many numbers were genuinely free to be anything.

Take the four dose effects. They are forced to add up to zero. So if I tell you the first three, the fourth is already decided — it has no freedom left. Four numbers, but only three were free. df for the signal = 3.

Now the noise. There are 40 fish. But we used the data to work out 4 group averages, and each average you calculate uses up one piece of freedom. 40 − 4 = 36.

Now divide each total by its own degrees of freedom, and the two become comparable:

total÷ df= average per unit
Signal26.8038.93
Noise56.47361.57

These per-unit averages are called mean squares, written MS. So MSTr = 8.93 and MSE = 1.57.

The number that reappears forever

MSE = 1.57 is your best estimate of how much fish vary for reasons other than the drug. Almost every calculation in the rest of the course divides by it. If you remember one number from this document, make it this one and what it means.

Step 6The verdict

Now the comparison the whole thing was built for. Divide signal by noise:

F = 8.93 ÷ 1.57 = 5.70 The signal is 5.7 times bigger than the noise, once both are measured fairly.
F "F"

Signal divided by noise. Named after the statistician Ronald Fisher.

F near 1 — signal is the same size as noise. Nothing to see.
F much bigger than 1 — signal towers over noise. Something is probably real.
F below 1 — the signal is smaller than the noise. Definitely nothing. You can answer instantly without any table.

But 5.70 is only impressive if luck could not easily have produced it. So: if the drug did absolutely nothing, how big would F get just by chance?

That question has a known answer. It looks like this.

Read this picture in three parts. The black curve is where F lands when nothing is happening — usually below 2. The red dashed line at 2.87 is the point beyond which luck only reaches 5% of the time. The green line at 5.70 is our fish. It is not just past the red line, it is far past it. To explain that by luck you would need a coincidence that happens about 3 times in 1000.
p-value "P value"

The chance of getting a result at least as extreme as yours if there were really no effect at all.

Ours is p = 0.0027, which is 0.27%, about 3 chances in 1000.

The usual cut-off is 0.05. Below that, people are willing to say the result is real. It is a convention, not a law of nature — there is nothing magic about 5%.

What a p-value is NOT

p = 0.0027 does not mean "there is a 99.73% chance the drug works". It is not the probability that your conclusion is right.

It says only this: if the drug did nothing, data like yours would be rare. That is grounds for disbelieving "the drug does nothing" — which is a slightly different, and weaker, statement than most people assume.

The whole thing on one table

Everything above is normally printed as four rows. This is what R gives you, and what an exam asks you to read or fill in:

The ANOVA table — trout
SourcedfSum SqMean SqFp
Sulfamerazine (signal)326.808.935.700.0027
Residuals (noise)3656.471.57
Total3983.27
You now understand every cell in that table

3 and 36 are how many numbers were free. 26.80 and 56.47 are squared-and-added arrows. 8.93 and 1.57 are those totals made comparable. 5.70 is one divided by the other. 0.0027 is how often luck manages that.

"Residuals" means noise. "ANOVA" just means "analysis of variance" — splitting variation into parts, which is exactly what we did in step 3.

Step 7Before you believe any of it

That p-value of 0.0027 was calculated by assuming three things about the fish. If any is badly false, the number is fiction and you would never know from looking at it.

The assumptionIn plain wordsHow you check
IndependenceOne fish's haemoglobin tells you nothing about another's. They are not sharing a tank and infecting each other.No plot can check this. You buy it by assigning fish to groups at random — which he did.
Equal spreadAll four dose groups are about equally variable.A plot called residuals vs fitted.
NormalityThe leftover randomness follows the familiar bell shape.A plot called a QQ plot.
Residual "re-sid-you-al"

A fish's leftover: how far it sits from its own group's average. It is the red line from step 3, written as a number.

The 5 g fish that measured 11.9 in a group averaging 9.33 has a residual of +2.57.

You cannot check assumptions on the raw measurements — you check them on the residuals. This matters, and it is the single most common mistake.

Check 1 — is the spread equal?

Plot each fish's leftover against what the model predicted for it. You want a shapeless cloud of equal thickness. You do not want a funnel.

Look at the vertical thickness as your eye travels left to right. On the left it stays about the same — good. On the right it starts thin and fans out — the dotted red guides trace the shape. That is called a funnel, and it means groups with bigger values are also more variable. When you see that, the p-value cannot be trusted.

Check 2 — is the randomness bell-shaped?

A QQ plot sounds intimidating and does something simple: it lines your leftovers up against what perfectly bell-shaped leftovers would look like. If they match, the dots fall on a straight line.

You are asking one question: do the dots follow the line? On the left, yes — with small wobbles at the ends, which is completely normal and expected. On the right the dots swing away upwards at the top. That means a few values are far larger than a bell curve allows: the data is lopsided, with a long tail to the right.

Check 3 — any single fish behaving impossibly?

Anything outside the red lines is worth investigating. The trout have nothing beyond ±3. The pollution data does. Do not simply delete an outlier — first ask whether it is a recording error, or a real and interesting phenomenon. If you do remove one, say so and report the analysis both with and without it.

What you do when a check fails

You do not give up. You usually change the scale.

The funnel is gone. A funnel means the spread grows in proportion to the size of the values — which happens when effects multiply rather than add. Taking logarithms turns multiplying into adding, so it flattens the fan. This one move very often fixes the spread problem and the lopsidedness at the same time, because they had the same cause.
One thing changes when you take logs

After a log transformation, a difference on the new scale is a ratio on the original scale.

If two cities differ by 1.27 on the log scale, that does not mean 1.27 units of chlorine. It means one has e1.27 = 3.6 times as much as the other. Always say which scale you are reporting on.

Step 8Which doses actually differ?

Our F-test said "something is going on". It did not say what. Your lecturer's phrase is worth keeping: the F-test tells you there is a fire, but not which room is burning.

The obvious move is to compare every pair of doses. With 4 groups there are 6 pairs. And here is the trap.

Why testing all 6 pairs is cheating

Each single test has a 5% chance of a false alarm. That sounds small. But run 6 of them and the chance that at least one raises a false alarm is 26%.

It is like dice. One roll rarely gives a six. Roll six times and a six becomes likely. Each test is a roll; a false alarm is the six.

With 10 groups — 45 pairs — the chance of at least one false alarm is 90%. You would be almost guaranteed to "discover" something that is not there.

The fix is a method that already accounts for how many comparisons you are making. For comparing all pairs, the standard tool is Tukey's test. It raises the bar just enough that the overall false-alarm rate stays at 5%.

This is the easiest plot in the course to read, and there is only one rule. If a bar crosses the red line at zero, that pair is not significantly different — because "no difference at all" is still a plausible answer. If a bar sits entirely to one side, that pair really does differ.
Reading it off
ComparisonDifferenceCrosses zero?Verdict
5 g vs 0 g+2.13noreally different
10 g vs 0 g+1.83noreally different
15 g vs 0 g+1.49only justborderline — cannot say
10 g vs 5 g−0.30yesno difference
15 g vs 5 g−0.64yesno difference
15 g vs 10 g−0.34yesno difference

Step 9What this means for the fish

Now translate the whole thing back into biology, which is the part that actually matters.

The finding

Every significant comparison involves the control group. No two treated groups differ from each other at all.

So the answer is: giving the drug raises haemoglobin, but the dose does not matter. 5 g works as well as 15 g.

That is genuinely useful — it says the farm should use the drug, and should use the smallest dose, since more costs money and buys nothing. The omnibus F-test alone could never have told you that. It only said "something differs".

The borderline row deserves care

15 g versus control came out at 1.49 with a threshold of about 1.51. It misses by 0.02.

Do not report that as "15 g has no effect". Report it as inconclusive, and say it was borderline. With a few more fish it would very likely have crossed. Treating a near-miss as a proven absence is one of the most common misreadings in science.

The complete story, in six sentences

Forty fish were split at random into four dose groups. Their haemoglobin varied a lot, even within a group. About a third of that variation lined up with which dose they got. Compared fairly against the background noise, that is 5.7 times more signal than you would expect from luck, which happens about 3 times in 1000 by chance. The assumptions behind that calculation were checked and held. Looking pair by pair, any dose beats no dose, but no dose beats any other.

Part twoThree more experiments, three new ideas

The trout story used one factor, chosen deliberately. Everything else in the course is a variation on it. Here are the three variations, each shown on real data.

Variation 1 — when you find nothing

A different experiment: six piglets, three diets, testing whether soya changes weight gain.

Compare the two panels. On the left the green bars barely move away from the blue line, and the dots are scattered widely around them — signal small, noise large, so F = 0.33 and p = 0.74. On the right the first group is clearly below the rest — F = 5.70, p = 0.0027. This is what "found something" versus "found nothing" actually looks like.
The sentence that loses marks

After the piglet result, do not write "soya has no effect on weight gain."

Write: "There is no significant evidence that diet affects weight gain (F = 0.33, p = 0.74). With only 2 piglets per group the study has very low power, so a real effect could easily have been missed."

Failing to find something is not the same as showing it is not there. A study with 2 animals per group could miss an elephant.

Power "power"

The chance your study will detect a real effect, if one exists.

It goes up when you measure more individuals, when the true effect is bigger, or when individuals are less variable. The piglet study has almost none — which is the real reason it found nothing.

Why more individuals help: individual animals never get less variable, but averages of several animals do. Average 10 fish and the wobble in your estimate is a tenth of what it was for one.

Variation 2 — when two things act at once

A barley trial: two soil types and two fertilisers, crossed so every combination is tried. Now you can ask a new kind of question — does the best fertiliser depend on the soil?

Ask only one thing of an interaction plot: are the lines parallel? On the left they are emphatically not — one fertiliser is much better on clay and slightly worse on sand. The lines cross. On the right they are much closer to parallel. Non-parallel means the effect of one factor depends on the other.
Interaction "in-ter-ac-tion"

The effect of one factor depends on the level of the other. In everyday language: "it depends".

With no interaction, effects simply stack — if clay is worth +2 and fertiliser 2 is worth +3, then clay with fertiliser 2 is worth +5. With an interaction, that combination is worth something else entirely.

Always test the interaction first. If it is real, you must not report the main effects on their own — there is no single honest answer to "is fertiliser 2 better?", because the true answer is "on clay yes, on sand no".

Variation 3 — when you do not care about the groups

The biggest conceptual jump in the course, and it is easier to see than to read.

A researcher picks 5 bulls at random from a national register of thousands, and measures milk yield in 8 daughters of each. He does not care about those 5 bulls. He wants to know: how much do bulls in general vary?

Compare how much the clouds overlap. On the left, a cow from bull 1 could easily out-produce a cow from bull 4 — knowing the father barely helps you predict the daughter. On the right, knowing the father would tell you almost everything. The number that measures this is the ICC, and for the real bulls it is 0.18 — 18% of the variation in milk yield is down to which bull the father was.
Fixed and random factors "fixed", "random"

Fixed — you chose the levels on purpose. Four doses of a drug. Repeat the study and you use the same four. Your conclusion applies only to those four.

Random — the levels are a sample from a big population. Five bulls out of thousands. Repeat the study and you get five different bulls. Your conclusion applies to the whole population.

The give-away phrases in an exam question are "randomly selected", "a random sample of", or r() around the name in R code.

The question changes too: with fixed factors you ask which level is best; with random factors you ask how much do levels vary.

Part threeThe picture gallery

Every graph you will meet, with what good and bad look like, and what to do about it. Use this when a plot appears in a question and you need to know what you are looking at.

Quick reference
PlotThe one question to askGoodBadIf it's bad
Boxplot
by group		 Are the boxes at different heights? Are they equally tall? Boxes similar height; heights differ if there's an effect One box far taller than the others Unequal spread — consider taking logs
Residuals vs fitted Does the vertical thickness stay the same left to right? Shapeless cloud, even thickness A funnel — thin at one end, wide at the other Take logs of the response and re-check
QQ plot Do the dots follow the straight line? Dots on the line; small wobbles at the ends are fine A systematic curve, especially swinging up at the top Take logs; or use a method that doesn't assume bell shapes
Standardised residuals Is anything outside ±3? Everything inside the lines One or more points beyond ±3 Investigate that individual — never just delete it
Interaction plot Are the lines parallel? Parallel — effects simply add up Crossing, converging or diverging Not "bad" — it's a finding. Report cell means, not main effects
Tukey plot Does each bar cross the zero line? Bar clear of zero = a real difference Bar crossing zero = no difference shown Nothing to fix — this is the answer
F distribution Is our F past the critical value? Far into the right tail = reject Under the hump = fail to reject F below 1 is never significant — answer instantly
The order these come in, always
  1. Boxplot — look before you calculate. Form an expectation.
  2. Fit the model, get the ANOVA table.
  3. Residuals vs fitted and QQ plot — are you allowed to believe the p-value?
  4. The F-test — is anything happening at all?
  5. Only if F rejects: Tukey, or planned comparisons, to find out what.
